blocks.x: You can just give your name first, who you are and when you were born, Jim.
You want the right name of Nathan or Jim Robinson? Yeah, everything about it. Your real name is Nathan. Nathan, yeah.
But you wouldn't want us to tell anybody.
Oh, see my professional name is Jim Robinson. See, everybody would say go by my professional name.
How did you get the name of Jim?
Well, people, you know, like they give people nicknames, you know, call them. Yeah. Because when the kids started calling you nicknames, they would just use it. So they would just stay like that way.
Where were you born?
Day Range, Louisiana.
That's down the river, on the other side?
On the other side, the LJ's side.
How close was that to Magnolia?
About three miles. About three miles from Magnolia.
Is that farther down the river than Magnolia?
That's Magnolia below me.
It's below you. What was the date when you were born?
December 25th. 18... 1890.
Did your parents play any music?
All my brothers, all my brothers played music.
Your brothers, how many brothers did you have?
I had three brothers beside myself. Were they all older?
The only ones that were older than me, I'm the youngest.
I'm the youngest in the family.
Did your father play anything?
No, my father was a Christian man.
Did he sing in the churches though?
He was a deacon of the church. And what would he do in the church? He was next to the preacher.
Would he lead the singing or anything?
No, he didn't sing. He sang when he was there.
I thought maybe he was featured or something.
No, no, no.
Sometimes I've seen the deacons in the Dr. Watts chants. They lead before the preacher gets there.
Oh yeah, but the deacon always takes the preacher's place. Not there. The deacon always takes the preacher place, you see. That's his position.
Was your church right down there near your home?
Oh, the church at Mahan.
How many people were in that town?
Oh, they had say about four or five hundred people.
Would there be any musical instruments in the church? Would they have a piano?
No, they have what they call the organ. They call it melodion years ago. They call it an organ now. Melodion. Melodion, melodion. That's for small.
With the pipes in there. With the pipes.
Do you remember any other music when you were young, when you were just a child there? Was there any band or dances?

Oh yeah, they had, at my home they had one of the best brass bands in the world. I mean, that country, you understand? They had one band at my home because Pace Unford grandfather took and taught that band. You see? That Day Range band. Magnolia band too. He was one taught son Henry and father. They had a band at Magnolia and one at your town. Oh yeah. Magnolia too, yeah.
Magnolia.
They had one at Magnolia, they had one at Day Range, they had one at Oakville. Oakville. Where is Oakville exactly?
That's before you get to Day Range.
That's before you get to Day Range. That's before you get to Day Range. That's before you get to Day Range. Five miles after you leave Belche, after you leave with that sea plan there.
Oh, one more thing. Where is St. Sophie?
St. Sophie is on this side of the river, but 30 miles on this side of the river.
And how far is that from Day Range?
Well that's, across the river. Just across the river? Just across the river, yeah. See, Day Range on the Algae side, St. Sophie on this side.
I was wondering because that's where Willie Parker is from.
Yeah, that's where St. Sophie is from.
And I just wondered how long he'd known you and all that.

Oh, Willie, Willie would have been known before I was born. Willie's, he was my oldest brother. How old is your oldest brother? My oldest brother, he's beautiful, Willie Parker, he's around his 80s or something odd. He's my oldest brother. Then I had two brothers of size, you understand, he was older than me.
Were they, say, 15 years or 20 years older than you or what? My brothers? Yes, how much older were they?
Oh, my brothers, we was two years apart. All two years? I mean nothing. Me and my other two brothers were three years apart, but my oldest brother was older, you understand? Was older.
What, 15 years you'd say or 20 or 10? What would you say?
Well, I couldn't imagine how my oldest brother, you understand, because I know he's Willie Parker.
Well, how would Sonny Henry compare with Willie Parker?
Well, Sonny and Willie, well I couldn't, he's dead, you understand, but I know they're around about the same age, you understand? Yeah.
You see?
Yeah.
It's so hard to figure out how old people are, you know, so the records got lost and everything, you know. What about the dance bands?
Did you go there and hear any dancers down in the country there? Oh, well. Even when you were a child from outside the hall, what kind of?

Well, they used to have bands from the city come down and play like, you know, orchestras play like, when they have little fairs and everything, you know. I was a small kid, I'd go around these, you had to, bands playing and everything.
Who were some of the people that came down there?
Well, Tom Albert used to come down all the time and play music. Tom Albert, he was well known, come down and play music.
Did he play trumpet or violin or what?
Tom was playing, Tom, once the first time he came and he was playing the violin, the next time he came and he was playing the trumpet.
Who else was with him? Do you remember who else was?
Well, some of the fellas, let me see. I remember once Frankie Dusen came with him once. Really? The trombone. Frankie Dusen came with him once.
Did Frankie Dusen ever teach music down there?
No, not to me, no.
I just wondered, huh? No.
Frankie never taught music. The only man who taught music down there when I knew it was Jim Mumphrey, the person for granddaddy. But he was the one who taught all them bands down there, Jim Mumphrey.
Would there be much difference between the Dairange band and the Magnolia band and say, Tom Albert's band? What would the difference be?
Well, I didn't find no difference because they all was playing the same type of music. What kind of music was that?
It was the marches.
It was all?
Six-eight.
One step, quick step, they were playing all different kinds of music. They didn't fool no, like that, like simple opera music, they didn't fool with that on the time. No, none of the classical.
No, no, that's classical.

But they had to like them, six-eight, them boys, just play that stuff, you know. Take twelve of them men and play as much as a big simple opera. How many were in a brass band? Well, it was, it was, it was 13 or 14, 14 men, I think. You see, at the time, they used the pecan. Yeah. Used the first tenor, solo alto, first alto, and used the, what am I saying? The tenor. Is that like the baritone horn? Yeah, like a baritone horn, I understand, a tenor. Is it upright? Upright, yeah, a tenor, I understand, upright. It may look a baritone, but it's not as big as a baritone horn. Yeah. You see, that's the time when them bands didn't have all them, like they got now, tenor sax, they used a baritone, just used them with baritone and clanny, you see? E flat clanny, they used all that kind of stuff. And E flat clanny. E flat clanny, yeah. E flat, yeah. E flat, and short one, E flat clanny.
How many trombones did they have in a band?
Well, they didn't use them with one trombone at a time. One trombone. One trombone. That was a val trombone, yeah. Val trombone. Used a tuba?
Yeah. Is it the upright horn?
No, upright, upright. Upright. Yeah, upright.
How many cornets?
Four, with trumpets. And drums?
Would they have drums?
Two drums. Snare drum and big drum. Bass drum.
And what kind of parades did they have? On what occasion did they put on a parade?

Well, for society it's a different thing, you know. Go to all different places, you know. Society got parades where they go, like, some of them all different places on a Sunday, different places. Did they ever play for a funeral down there?
Well, no, they never had food with that.
No, no, I suppose they never had food with that. No, no, no, they never had food with that. Well, where would they play? Would they always march? Would they sit down?
Would they play inside?

Oh, they would, like, they would rehearse, like that, they would sit down, but every time they had a rehearsal, they would make a parade around the village, different places, make a parade, you see. They would keep them trimmed, you see. Walked by the mall going, the mall coming, you see.
Did people dance to the music? Oh, sure. So, were they playing a dance hall?
They could play in a dance hall, yeah, sure.
And what would they play then? Would they play the 6-8 march?

No, no, no, they'd play all the different songs. Oh, I see. Yeah, different songs. The brass band would be in the dance hall. Yeah, yeah, the brass band, yeah. Play the dance hall. Yeah, yeah, sure. They'd play different songs. Would they play hymns ever? They'd play hymns on the church, they'd play like that, in the church, you see.
Would the band go inside the church? Yeah, the band, sure.

I've seen the young tuxedo do that, yeah. I've seen Eureka. Yeah, they go to the church. They would play for collection? Yeah. And how would they take up the collection? The basket, the basket in the churches, no?
Would the members march, or would they pass it?
No, Everybody was sitting in the seat. Oh, I see. And the fellow go around with the basket, pass it, and they put them in the church.
Well, did we ask what kind of a church your father was digging? Baptist. Baptist, I thought, sorry. I didn't know if we had it down. Baptist, yeah.
I thought it could have been Methodist.
Did they have a Methodist church down there, too?
Oh, yeah, they had a Methodist church down there. Methodist, Catholic, all that.
Were most of the people down there Methodist or Catholic?
Well, it's all half and half. About half and half. Half and half.
Did you ever get up to the Magnolia plant? Was it more of a plantation or a town?
A plantation, yeah.
Was there a little settlement there, stores and all that?
No, they had a big refounder there. Used to refound the sugar and stuff.
Did you ever get up there to hear their band?

Oh, yeah, sure, I heard that band. I was small. That band used to come home any time, you know? Like this band come home on Sunday, and then during this band, we would go down to Magnolia, you know what I'm saying? Well, they're all the same professors and was teaching us, you know what I'm saying?
Who were some of the people in the bands down there?

Oh, well, I'll tell you, a lot of them people is dead. I couldn't remember all them people's names. I just thought you could tell us- But Sonny could tell you all them fellas' names, because he used to play in that band with him,
you know? I thought maybe some of them were here, you could tell us where to find them, you know?
Oh, no, them fellas. Almost one fella I knew who played that band, he was called Riffith Harrison Bones. Oh, he was in that band. Yeah, he was in that band. He was playing trumpet.
Was it in the Deer Range or the Magnolia?
No, Magnolia band.
And are the Deer Range fellas along?
No, all them fellas is dead.
Everyone?
All them fellas just playing that band, all them fellas is dead.
What is Deer Range like today? What kind of a town is it?

It's nothing but water now. Nothing then? They had a crevasse there. A ship run through the levee in high water, and this ruined the whole Paris down there. That's it. Nothing but water, nothing but water. Nothing but a duck paw now. You see? People, that's where they do all the hunting down there.
That's all I knew is hunting.
It's my home and I get there with that water.
What was it when you lived there?
Farming area? Yeah, yeah, farming, yeah. Big farm. Sugar cane? Sugar cane, yeah.
What would they do in the fields when they were working? Would anybody ever sing? Sing.
Whistling like the fellas do here, singing, just whistling. What would they sing and whistle? Oh, some sing hymns, some whistle songs, whatever they wanted to do.
Do you remember any of the ones that you used to sing when you were a little boy?
Oh, I forgot them things. A lot of things I was a boy I used to do. I forgot them things.
What was the first band you ever played with yourself?
First band I played was with, you mean I played with?
Yes.
Oh, the first band I played was with Auguste. We had a band here, I.S.M. Morgan.
Tell me first, what instrument did you start on?
I started on guitar first. I started on guitar. And what would you do?
Would you play chords or would you pick up? I'd play chords.

Did you pick it all with your fingers? No, just playing and rapping chords. Did you have a teacher or did you pick it up yourself? I picked it up myself, yeah. Do you remember where you got your instrument? Oh, my, when I got an instrument, I was around about 15 years of age.
Did you have to earn the money or somebody give it to you?

Well, my sister bought it for me. She bought it. See, because my other worst fellow had guitar around there. I used to like to play so much, so she went and bought me a guitar. I just took it and played it, you see. Then the fellow, Javon, he used to come home, but he used to stay by my sister's house, you know, you understand. He'd come and give lessons. He'd stay there, but he used to show me the chords and everything. But he liked me a lot of himself, you see.
Did you sing when you played guitar?

No, I never could sing, Dick. But I could play good guitar. Yeah, I could pick all them songs I could. And what about? Pick games and different things. But now I can't play nothing. I forgot about it. That's true. I can make a few chords, but. When did you pick up trombone then? I took up trombone in 1970.
Where were you? In France.
In France. I was in, in Bush, France. Bush. Yeah.
Did you join the, that was pretty early, wasn't it? Were you drafted or did you?

No, they drafted. They drafted. Yeah. Yeah. So how did they come pick up trombone? Which the lieutenant was, he wanted the band, you know, for the company. And so he asked them, any fellas had an idea they wanted to take apart in music. Well I knew I could play guitar, but I didn't put no trombone. So they had a fellas from Paulianville, or Onis Heims, he's from Boerleg, he's played in the Claiborne Williams band, well they were a good musician. Willie Foster, well he was from here, and he was a good musician. So he told me, I said, Willie, he called me Bob, he said, I said, I'm a good musician.

Bob said, man, come on, we'll take a tram on. We learn you how to play. I said, oh man, I don't want to fool nothing like that. He said, man, you see who done took the raffles from us? He said, no, I said, listen, you got to shovel, you got to pick. You got to handle both them things. You got to dig a hole and shovel all that, that, that. I said, man, that's true, too. He said, look, every day. And we had them big heavy shoes on, and that again, them fellas was in the band, nice, them nice Army Ruskin shoes, you know, light shoes, keep them shining, nice leg. I said, oh, I'm going to get on this stuff myself.
They didn't have to work hard then, huh?
No, just go to the YMC and this every day in rehearsal. So in that morning when they called the roll, understand, I stepped on up, I just took a chance.
I took a chance, man, walk up there.

Lieutenant, Fire Lieutenant, they named Lieutenant Lyons, too. I said, all right, Robson, you want to play trombone? I said, yes, sir. I said, all right. I said, well, give me a brand new chord on trombone. So I just took it and put it together, you know. But I could pull it up, understand? Well, every day, so after, they had a fella who was working with the band, but it was three or four weeks, and he couldn't even pull his horn up. You know, and I just, every day, I just would take him, and after rehearsal, I would take him down behind the hill, you know, and show him how to handle his position, you see, you know what I mean? So after that, so I just take me and him both, you know.
Yeah.

Every day after that, you know, behind the hills and feet together, have the trombone, and I just have his hand and show him how to put the position. And after that, I said, but two weeks time, I thought I'd run my scales, you know. And this fella, he couldn't blow nothing.
Did Willie Foster help you much?

Yeah, Willie Foster, yeah. Willie had to lead the violin, had his violin, and every day, when I get a chance, you know, I'd go by Willie with his violin, he'd play a song for me, and I'd take the trombone, it was vamp, you know, he'd show him what to make with this vamp. And then I got to doing that, and so everything went on fine. So the other time I played, he wasn't doing nothing so much, and so they had us both in the band together, you know, playing in a jazz band. Yeah. But he just confused because he couldn't play that by making all the chords. So Lieutenant Lyons said, well, I think the best, we got to put this fella back in the big band and let Jim play by himself, you understand, in the small band. Yeah, in the small band. And man, after that, I went on, after that, yeah. Like to me, that thing just come to me overnight. I swear to Christ, that trombone, come to me overnight. You know, my whole heart and mind had got hurt. And like this come to me, this overnight. And man, we went out there, and three weeks time, man, we gone all over France, playing for the lieutenants, for the buck private. The buck private treat you better than lieutenants there, because you get more money from the buck private. Just boil the liquor you want and different stuff. And the lieutenants, sometimes they'll give you a good pay, sometimes they'll give you nothing. Yeah, man, that's, I went out a lot, I see a lot of friends.
Anybody else in that band that you remember from New Orleans? Just Willie Foster, anybody else? Willie Foster, let me see.
Willie had a bunch of fellas from New Orleans, but he wasn't playing in the band, you know. Yeah. Those fellas was overseas with me, you know. I wasn't in the band, though.
No, they wasn't in the band.
I meet the Latin fellas right now, and I go downtown. All the way around, back, St. Bernard Street. Yeah. I made a bunch of them. It's the last time I was down there for the meeting.
Did you stay in France until the war was all over then?
No, man, I stayed in France, say, but, to France 18 months. 18 months. 18 months. 18 months. I took so long, I hadn't thought he was going to send me back home.
Did you learn any French over there? I couldn't say nothing.

I'll tell you one thing, but then people, I got rid of it with my American money, because you see, I couldn't count their money, so I'd give them my American dollar, and so they used to give me any kind of change of that money, you understand? I didn't know what it was, but they liked that American dollar. Well, because they'd run you down for American dollar.
Say, can you hum a little vamp for me? I was wondering what kind of vamp you learned when Willie Foster would play the violin. They're going to play now?
Yeah.
Well, just hum a couple of little licks for me. Can you do it?

You're talking about the vamp style, what is that? I mean, is it the bass style? That's a vamp style. Ba-ba-ba-ba-ba-ba-ba-ba-ba-ba-ba-ba-ba-ba-ba-ba-ba-ba-ba-ba-ba-ba-ba-ba-ba-ba-ba-ba-ba-ba-ba-ba-ba-ba-ba-ba. That's a vamp, you see? They're fitting in, you know?
Like you say in Thailand Especially when a trumpet player holds a good lead like Heart Society, I'd rather vamp the part than trying to sing a solo, understand? Because it's a song much better.
I've heard you talk before years ago about the importance of the rhythm. That is, you have to have that beat on the trombone. Can you tell us about that?

Yeah, that beat. You see, that beat on the trombone. In other words, you see, when you play this language, you can't rush it. If you rush it, you can't make your chord thing good, understand? See, because you rush in those two, see? Now, especially like our band, Sam, like the band he got there now. But our band, this band never played like Sam Morgan band. Because see, Sam had a tempo. He set you to a tempo and that rhythm holds you right there. You never move. See? Because that's a whole background. Under that piano, your drum, bass, and banjo. That's your background. Now, if them people don't write together, you can go to your bands out there. You can't even get nowhere. Now, Bill, you know I'm telling the truth. Yeah, I know. You see? Now, that band, and the drum, boom, boom. You're going as fast as a cycle. You can't execute your own like you want to. It's too fast. Understand? But along that drum and that piano, that band, and bass, it must work together. Well, that's the whole thing. That's where any man got a band should get that together, that drum and bass and banjo. Understand? And piano. Because that's the main thing. That's your background. And at that clicking, your band got to go right.
Well, how would they work with Sam Morgan?

Listen, Sam was on the time because Sam had one of them slapsticks, you see? You see? And Sam would get that band to move. He'd hold that stick. Like, understand? But otherwise, the band, the father had got together, so the rhythm, he had to worry about because this dude, you knock a piece off. You couldn't move them, brother. They're still right there. You couldn't move them. No, you couldn't move them. You couldn't move them. And Sam would take any kind of number and make a really, a dance number of it. You don't care what kind of number, but he'd take it and make a dance number. He could put a time to play in a moving time that you'd like it. He was a good man for that. Otherwise, we have one of the best, I mean, swing bands in the city of New Orleans. In the world, I'll tell you that. At Sam Morgan, we had to swing to that band because otherwise, you come to that band, no care what you could play. Don't say that with the music proposition, but that swing. You ought to do that swing. You see, some brothers, they've been playing so fast, they get the swing band, they can't play like they want to. You see? You see? They don't, someone move their finger on their horn and different things, and that's, that's make it sound bad.
When did you join Sam Morgan? That was your first job, you said, I believe.
I got in Sam's band in 1922. 22.
Who was the leader then?

Sam. No, the first band, his brother Isaiah Morgan, but Sam, Sam here, his band, his band, the Magnolia band, he had, well, they had a split, you see. Sam had a stroke and he got sick, well, the band split, you see. And after Sam got out, got well, well, he come with his brother and put the band on the Sam name because he had all the work and everything, you know. He's more famous. Put everything in his hand.
So now you joined Isaiah first.
Yeah.
About what year was that?
That was 1920.
1920. You'd just gotten back from France, I guess, a little while ago.
Oh, yeah, I just got from the old sea.
When did you move up to New Orleans?
Yeah, New Orleans. I came, I live from 1911.
Mm-hmm. 1911.
What kind of work did you do before? You were old enough to work then, weren't you?
Oh, yes, I worked. When I first came to New Orleans, I went to work at the Southern Mississippi. Stewardship Company.
Yeah, Stewardship Company.
I went to work there. I worked there until the time I went to work. I was a very young, young, young man. I came in New Orleans.
Yes.
And let me see what we was making the day for getting, we was making 3.30 a day and making 4.40 that night. Well, that was a big side then for my fellow then.
What did you make in the country?
Huh?
How much money would you make out in the country?
Well, we'd make a dollar a day in the country. That's a big percentage, wasn't it? Yeah. That's what I said. In the country, I got money. You have to spend much money down there.
And what kind of work were you doing in the country?
Oh, well, we used to work in the field, different places like that, you know?
I was wondering about those, you mentioned there were guitar players around their range, huh?
Oh, they had plenty of guitar players around there. They had plenty of fellas who played guitars, you know?
And what would they play?
What would they play? Like I played blues and different things, songs? Different things that were?
Would they be finger-picking style? Would they be chord?

Oh, some of them was chord. Some of them was better players than what I was, you see? Yeah. Oh yeah, better players than what I was. Because I'd come up after them, learning after them, you know? And some of them could play better than me. Then after I'd beat some of them, I'd beat them playing, you know?
Could they play melody?
Oh yeah, sure.
Would they sing?
Oh yeah, some of them could sing. Some of them used to have a harmonica, to let this wire over their mouth, understand? And play the harmonica, and play the guitar too.
And you don't remember any of the names of the songs?
Oh, well them old songs, the Steamboat Bill, all that come on numbers, and Casey John, all them numbers was out there, you know?
And the blues? What kind of blues?
Well, much blues then at the time then.
What about blues?

It wasn't much of a blues then, understand? There's no part of what blues that much. Not as many blues then? No, no, not like now. Blues ain't been long, just a few years been out, people was playing the blues and all like it. It wasn't proper like the time I came up, you know?
I wondered, when was the first brass band on the street that you played?
I played the first brass band I played was for the Jefferson Buzzard, it was on the Carmel Day, with Willie Parker.
Willie Parker.
He got the job for me.
Is that the Eureka band or what kind of, any name for it?
I believe that was the Magnolia band I think. I think it was the Magnolia band. I think it was.
Did you ever play with the Terminal band? No, no, no.
I never played with that band.
Can you tell us a bit more about the Sam or the Isaiah Morgan band? Who else was in that band when you joined?

Oh, they had, you see, Oyl Fushey, my nephew Sidney Brown, Andrew Morgan, Johnny Dave, Shine, Sam Morgan, Isaiah and myself. And we just knew that woman, May, Piano, May. Sometimes we used Piano, you know, May, May, Piano.
Who else did you use on Piano later?
Sometimes we used to use George E. Parker, you know, when May couldn't go to town, you know, we used George E. Parker.
Did you ever use clarinet much in that band?
Oh, yeah. Did Andrew double it? No, no. Yeah, Andrew used to play the clarinet and Oyl would play soprano. Oyl would play soprano.
Would there be any rule? Would they play those two together and then play alto and tenor together? Or would they play soprano and tenor?
No, they play together, understand? Like it's a special chorus like that, you know, they play for clarinet and sax, well, they play soprano, they play together, understand?
Would they play alto and clarinet at the same time?
No, they play alto and tenor.
Alto and tenor.
That would sound better. Yeah, alto and tenor. Alto and tenor.
When did Sam have his stroke? Do you remember about him?

Let's see. Sam had his stroke, his first stroke. Sam had his first stroke, I believe, in 19... His first stroke, I believe, in 19... His first stroke, I believe, in 19... 20... 20... 20... 20... 20...
I think.
I think, 1928, I think Sam had his first stroke.
And after he got well, what happened?

Sam had his first stroke, yeah, in 1928, I think, Bill, because he took his second stroke... No, for a while. Sam had his first stroke, I believe, in 1926. Must have been... 26, yeah. Because they made those records.
26, because in 1928, we went to Chicago. Yeah.

You see, because he had got well, we went to Chicago. And after we came out of Chicago, in 1929, he took his other stroke. You see, that's right. Did you travel much, besides that trip to Chicago, go any place else? Oh yeah, we used to go all to Mississippi, Alabama. All to Mississippi, Alabama, but the West Coast, we never went to the West Coast much, you understand?
Did you get to New York at all?
No, we didn't go to New York. We went to Chicago.
I was on the excursion. On the excursion.
Yeah, on the excursion.
Did you play on the train or?
We played on the train and we played at the Warwick's Hall in Chicago.
Warwick?
I hate to change the subject but I see the tapes better. Did any of your uncles or grandparents or grand uncles play?
All my brothers used to play music.
But no others, huh?
No, no, no.
Your mother, did she?
No, no, my mother died a small kid. I thought maybe she was an organ player. No, I just remember my mother, I was a small kid and she died.
What did your brothers play?
One of my brothers played trombone. The oldest one played trombone. And the next one played bass and the other one played cyclophon.
And their names?
Sam Robertson.
He was a trombone brother?

No, he was the cyclophon player. Another brother named Effie, Effie Robertson. He was the bass player. Effie? Effie. Effie. My oldest brother played trombone. And his name? His name Sparks. Sparks. Yeah.
When did the saxophone come out for your brother to play?
